content.content:
1	Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations frequently has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports all have to be attached to a run of pipe that is already installed and often still in service. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.
2	
3	A split frame creates a mechanical difficulty that a one piece collar does not have. The tightening motion has to be delivered across the split line. The common answer is to draw the two frame halves toward one another, typically with a bolt, a toggle or a band, so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe. Because the closing force enters the frame at the split line, the grip is concentrated near the split and falls away around the arc, the frame is deformed in service, and the load carried by the clamp reacts back into the closure hardware. When the clamp is meant to hold a measuring head in a repeatable position, that uneven and closure dependent grip is a direct source of error, and repeated opening and closing does not return the head to the same place.
4	
5	A second approach fits the frame with individually adjustable jaws or screws that are wound in against the pipe one at a time. That approach decouples the grip from the split line, but it requires a tool, it requires the operator to balance the jaws by feel, and it is slow. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed off the axis of the frame, thin walled pipe can be dented, and the clamp is again seated differently each time it is fitted.
6	
7	Clamps of both kinds are also usually sized for a nominal pipe diameter, so a technician has to carry a set of clamps and identify the correct one before working. Flat or nominally curved jaw faces bear on a pipe of any other diameter along an edge rather than over an area.
8	
9	Finally, an operator working with a quick acting latch has no reliable way of knowing how hard the clamp has been applied. A latch that snaps shut gives the same tactile feel whether the jaws have seated properly on the pipe, whether the pipe is at the small end of the range and the jaws have barely reached it, or whether the mechanism has been over travelled. Torque measurement is available for a bolted clamp but not for a latch, and a diameter reading indicates only the size of the pipe rather than the load the clamp is carrying.
10	
11	There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe of a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, that does not take its grip from the split line, and that tells the operator mechanically when the clamping load has reached the intended range.
12

1	A reusable split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the tightening motion is not transmitted through the split line of the frame but through a cam ring that is itself split, and which is reassembled into a working ring by the act of closing the frame.
2	
3	The clamp has a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and joined at a latch end by a releasable latch, so that the frame halves can be swung apart, placed around a pipe that is already installed, and closed again. A plurality of jaw carriages is distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. Each jaw carriage is slidable in a radial guide of the frame and carries a jaw pad that is mounted on the jaw carriage for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface to the pipe. Because each jaw pad pivots, it seats itself on the pipe surface it meets, and the clamp is not restricted to one nominal pipe diameter.
4	
5	A cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. The cam ring is segmented. A first cam-ring segment is carried by the first frame half and a second cam-ring segment is carried by the second frame half, so each segment stays with its own frame half when the clamp is opened. The first cam-ring segment and the second cam-ring segment have complementary drive faces at the hinge end and complementary drive faces at the latch end. Closing the frame halves brings those complementary drive faces into engagement and couples the cam-ring segments so that they move together as one cam ring about the pipe. Closure of the frame is therefore what creates the drive train, and no separate coupling step is asked of the operator.
6	
7	Each jaw carriage carries a follower that is received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. The latch carries a wedge. Moving the latch drives the wedge against a ring drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled cam ring through a limited stroke about the pipe. Each oblique slot converts that common rotation into inward travel of its own jaw carriage, so that all of the jaw carriages advance together by an amount fixed by the geometry of the slots rather than by the judgment of the operator. A carriage spring biases each jaw carriage outward, so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws before the frame halves are opened. The clamping load is taken by the cam ring in the annular guide rather than across the split line, and the latch is not asked to hold the working load through the frame joint.
8	
9	The latch has a first position in which it holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which it drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. The two positions separate the act of capturing the pipe from the act of loading the jaws, so the operator can position the clamp along the pipe while the frame is already captive.
10	
11	A force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive path between a latch handle of the latch and the wedge. Once all of the jaw pads have contacted the pipe, further travel of the latch handle to the over-center position is absorbed by compression of the force-limiting spring stack instead of forcing one jaw farther than the others. The remaining latch travel is therefore taken up by a defined elastic element, the clamping load is bounded by that element, and a pipe that sits anywhere within the range of the clamp is gripped by a load set by the spring stack rather than by where the latch happens to reach its stop.
12	
13	An indicator pin coupled to the force-limiting spring stack moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing of the latch when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a visible mechanical report that the clamp is loaded within that range. The indicator reports clamp loading and does not measure pipe diameter.
14	
15	The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool or a conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages, so a load applied to the mounting boss is carried by the frame and does not disturb the cam drive.
16	
17	A method of clamping a pipe and a method of releasing the clamp are also disclosed, in which the frame halves are closed about the pipe to couple the cam-ring segments, the latch is moved to the first position and then to the over-center position to rotate the coupled cam ring, and the residual latch travel is absorbed in the force-limiting spring stack.

input.summary: The draft is internally coherent in its naming and its mechanics, and the four figure briefs agree with each other and with the numeral table (12 = upper half / first cam-ring segment 32 at upper left, 14 = lower half / second segment 34 at bottom; hinge end = left = faces 44/46; latch end = right = faces 48/50). No pixel-level figure review was possible: figures/ contains only the four Markdown briefs, there are no rendered-*.png files, and review/figure-audit-evidence.json does not exist in this workspace, so every figure finding below is against the brief text only. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references ("(none)") and the draft contains no [REF:...] citation, so there is no citation fidelity defect to report — but the Background's characterisations of bolt/toggle/band closures, individually wound jaws and nominal-diameter clamps rest on no source in the workspace, and the art supplied to this draft may be incomplete. The dominant problem is disclosure fidelity: the inventor's disclosure and the single-message conversation are one page long and identical to one another, yet the detailed description adds a substantial layer of structure, alternatives, load paths and performance results that neither source states — an over-center link (numeral 68, claimed in claim 5), a 2-into-1 split of the radial guides between frame halves (claim 8), a pad pivot axis orientation (claim 14), a roller follower (claim 15), indicator-pin mounting detail (claim 4), stroke-limiting structures (claim 12), a drive lug on the cam ring that also drives the FIG. 3 geometry, and several asserted results (self-centering, load reaction away from the split line, spring-stack preload relationship, positioning along the pipe in the first latch position, claim 22). Ten dependent claims and one method claim rest on those additions. Claim/description terminology drift ("closed condition", "assembly", "uncoupled", "resisted") and one antecedent-basis slip in claim 9 are minor by comparison.

findings.title: Over-center link 68 is a structural element no source discloses, and claim 5 recites it
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶43; draft/09-claims.md claim 5; draft/numerals.md numeral 68; figures/fig-04.md
findings.detail: The disclosure describes only a latch position: "a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe", and it places the spring stack directly "between the latch handle and the wedge". The candidate converts the over-center *position* into a discrete over-center *link* that is a member of the latch, gives it a numeral, claims it, and draws it in FIG. 4. Neither disclosure.md nor conversation.md mentions any link, bar or connecting member between the handle and the spring stack. This is candidate-introduced structure, and the FIG. 4 brief's "short straight bar" exists only because the draft invented it.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶43: "the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58, a force-limiting spring stack 62 and an over-center link 68. ... the over-center link 68 connects the latch handle 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 62." Claim 5: "wherein the releasable latch further comprises an over-center link connecting the latch handle to the force-limiting spring stack." fig-04.md: "Inside the housing, a link drawn as a short straight bar connected at its upper end to the handle by a small circle spaced from that joint, and at its lower end to the upper plate by a small circle." Disclosure: "A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge".
findings.fix: Delete "and an over-center link 68" and the clause "and the over-center link 68 connects the latch handle 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 62" from ¶43; delete claim 5 and renumber; delete numeral 68 from numerals.md; delete the link bullet and numeral 68 from figures/fig-04.md (leaving the handle joined to the housing and the spring stack in the drive path, which the disclosure does support).

findings.title: Two-guides-in-one-half / one-in-the-other distribution is unsupported, and claim 8 recites it
findings.detail: The disclosure says only that "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame." It says nothing about how the three are apportioned between the two frame halves, and nothing about each half being loaded by the clamping action. The candidate supplies a specific 2/1 apportionment, presents it as the illustrated form, states a consequence, and claims it.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶15: "In the illustrated form two of the radial guides 24 are formed in one of the frame halves and a remaining one of the radial guides 24 is formed in the other frame half, so that each frame half carries at least one jaw carriage 22 and each frame half is loaded by the clamping action." Claim 8: "wherein two of the radial guides are formed in one of the first frame half and the second frame half and a remaining one of the radial guides is formed in the other of the first frame half and the second frame half."
findings.fix: Delete that sentence from ¶15 and delete claim 8, renumbering. The disclosed statement "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame" is already carried by ¶9 and claim 7.

findings.title: Widening from the disclosed three carriages to "more than three", plus an added three-point rationale
findings.detail: The disclosure fixes the count at three: "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame." It offers no other number and no reason for three. The candidate adds both a rationale ("stable seat ... without over constraining") and an express additional embodiment having more than three carriages, which is the disclosure basis on which claim 1's "a plurality of jaw carriages" rests. Neither source supports either sentence.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶9: "Three carriages define a stable seat on a round pipe without over constraining it. The synchronizing relationship described below is not limited to that number, and a clamp having more than three jaw carriages 22 is built in the same way, each additional jaw carriage 22 being coupled to the cam ring by its own follower and its own oblique slot as described below."
findings.fix: Delete both sentences from ¶9, leaving "In the form shown in FIG. 1 the plurality of jaw carriages 22 consists of three jaw carriages 22 distributed about the closed frame."

findings.title: Jaw-pad pivot axis orientation is unsupported, and claim 14 recites it
findings.detail: The disclosure states only that each carriage "carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe". It never states the axis about which the pad pivots or its orientation relative to the pipe. The candidate names a "pad axis", fixes it parallel to the pipe axis, and claims that orientation.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶17: "The pad axis is parallel to the axis of the pipe 20 in the illustrated form". Claim 14: "wherein each jaw pad pivots about a pad axis parallel to the central axis." Disclosure: "carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter."
findings.fix: Delete the pad-axis sentence from ¶17 and delete claim 14, renumbering; retain the disclosed "mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement" phrasing, which is supported.

findings.title: Roller follower is unsupported, and claim 15 recites it
findings.detail: The disclosure says only "Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring." It gives no form for the follower. The candidate supplies a three-way menu of forms and then claims one of them (a roller) as a dependent limitation. The description cannot supply its own support for a detail the candidate introduced.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶33: "The follower 40 may be a pin, a roller on a pin, or a block." Claim 15: "wherein each follower comprises a roller."
findings.fix: Delete the follower-form sentence from ¶33 and delete claim 15, renumbering.

findings.title: Indicator-pin mounting and housing opening are unsupported, and claim 4 recites them
findings.detail: The disclosure gives only the indicator's behaviour: "A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range." It does not say the pin is carried by the movable end of the stack, that the housing has an opening, that the pin passes through it, or that the pin emerges past the fixed edge. The candidate adds all four, claims them in claim 4, and draws the opening and the projecting rod in FIG. 4.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶47: "The indicator pin 64 is carried by the movable end of the force-limiting spring stack 62 and projects through an opening of the latch housing 58 ... the emergence of the indicator pin 64 past the fixed edge 60 is a visible mechanical report". Claim 4: "wherein the indicator pin is carried by a movable end of the force-limiting spring stack and projects through an opening of the latch housing." fig-04.md: "Its top wall is a horizontal line interrupted by a small opening"; "an indicator pin drawn as a slender vertical rod ... passing through the small opening in the top wall and projecting a short distance above it."
findings.fix: In ¶47 delete the sentence beginning "The indicator pin 64 is carried by the movable end" and change "the emergence of the indicator pin 64 past the fixed edge 60" to "the position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60"; delete claim 4 and renumber; in figures/fig-04.md delete the top-wall opening and reduce the pin bullet to a rod whose visible end stands adjacent the top wall (numeral 60 can target the top wall edge, 64 the visible rod end).

findings.title: Stroke-limiting structures are unsupported, and claim 12 recites one of them
findings.detail: The disclosure states that the latch "rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke" but never says what bounds that stroke. The candidate supplies three candidate bounding structures — including a stop face of the annular guide, which appears nowhere else in the draft or in either source — and claims the slot-end variant.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶39: "The limited stroke is bounded by the frame, by the ends of the oblique slots 38, or by a stop face of the annular guide 36, so that the cam ring 30 cannot be driven beyond the working range of the jaw carriages 22." Claim 12: "wherein the limited stroke is bounded by ends of the oblique slots." Disclosure: "rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke."

findings.title: Drive lug and inclined ring drive face added to legitimize FIG. 3 geometry
findings.detail: The disclosure says only that "Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring". It does not describe a lug projecting from a segment, does not say the face is inclined to the wedge path, and does not attribute the face to the latch-end of a particular segment. The FIG. 3 brief nonetheless draws a lug on the lower segment with an inclined flank and targets numeral 54 at that flank, and ¶39 supplies text for exactly that invented geometry.

findings.title: Asserted load path — grip reaction taken around the whole arc rather than across the split line
findings.detail: Neither source says anything about where the clamping reaction is carried, about the latch not holding the working load, or about the annular guide distributing reaction around the arc. The disclosure's statement of what the invention does is limited to coupling, driving, synchronizing and force limiting. This asserted structural result is the draft's central advantage narrative and it traces to nothing in the inventor's material.
findings.evidence: Summary ¶7: "The clamping load is taken by the cam ring in the annular guide rather than across the split line, and the latch is not asked to hold the working load through the frame joint." Draft ¶23: "Because the annular guide 36 continues around both frame halves, the reaction to the clamping load is taken by the frame around the whole arc rather than across the split line between the frame halves." Summary ¶1: "the tightening motion is not transmitted through the split line of the frame but through a cam ring that is itself split". Disclosure (whole statement of effect): "closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel."
findings.fix: Delete the quoted sentence from Summary ¶7 and the "Because the annular guide 36 continues around both frame halves..." sentence from ¶23; in Summary ¶1 state only that the cam ring is itself split and is reassembled by closing the frame, which the disclosure supports.

findings.title: Self-centering, slot-inclination trade-off and diameter-range results are unsupported
findings.detail: The disclosure never states that the clamp centers an off-centre pipe, never relates slot inclination to clamping force or mechanical advantage, and never says the useful diameter range is set by total radial travel. All three are engineering results the candidate supplies. The disclosure's only statement about diameter range is that the pivoting pad bears on a pipe "without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter".
findings.evidence: Draft ¶35: "Where the pipe 20 is not exactly centered when the frame is closed, the jaw pad 26 that reaches the pipe first begins to center the pipe within the frame ... The inclination of the oblique slots 38 may be chosen to trade stroke against mechanical advantage, a shallower inclination giving a larger clamping force for a given drive force and a smaller radial travel for a given rotation, and the useful range of pipe diameters for a given clamp is set by the total radial travel available at the jaw carriages 22."
findings.fix: Delete ¶35 in its entirety; the synchronization statement it elaborates is already fully set out in ¶33 in disclosure-supported terms.

findings.title: Spring-stack preload relationship and thin-wall deformation result are unsupported
findings.detail: The disclosure states only that additional handle travel after all pads contact the pipe "compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others". It says nothing about the stack transmitting drive without compressing before contact, nothing about the carriage-spring resistance being small relative to the stack preload (a design constraint that would have to be satisfied for the described behaviour), and nothing about comparable loads across the size range or about thin-walled pipe.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶45: "Until all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, the force-limiting spring stack 62 transmits the drive from the latch handle 56 to the wedge 52 substantially without compressing, because the resistance of the carriage springs 42 is small compared with the preload of the force-limiting spring stack 62. ... so the same clamp applies a comparable load to a large pipe and to a small pipe within its range, and a thin walled pipe is not deformed by the surplus travel of the latch."
findings.fix: Delete the first sentence of ¶45 and the trailing clause beginning "so the same clamp applies a comparable load"; retain the disclosed sentences about further handle travel compressing the stack and the load being set by the stack rather than by the latch stop.

findings.title: Positioning the clamp along the pipe in the first latch position is unsupported, and claim 22 recites it
findings.detail: The disclosed installation sequence is: open the latch, swing the halves apart, place them around a pipe, close the frame, move the latch to the holding position, then move it to the over-center position. There is no step of sliding, rotating or stationing the clamp along the pipe while the latch is in the first position, and no statement that the first position permits it. The candidate adds that step in three places and makes it a method claim.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶41: "The first position allows the operator to capture the pipe 20 and slide or rotate the split pipe clamp 10 to its intended station before any clamping load is applied." ¶51: "and positions the split pipe clamp 10 along the pipe 20." Summary ¶9: "so the operator can position the clamp along the pipe while the frame is already captive." Claim 22: "further comprising positioning the split pipe clamp along the pipe while the releasable latch stands in the first position and before the releasable latch is moved to the over-center position." Disclosure: "closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position."
findings.fix: Delete the quoted sentence from ¶41, delete "and positions the split pipe clamp 10 along the pipe 20" from ¶51, delete the trailing clause of Summary ¶9 after "loading the jaws", and delete claim 22, renumbering.

findings.title: Menus of materials, forms and alternatives that neither source discloses
findings.detail: Seven separate passages supply construction alternatives for parts the disclosure names but never characterises. The disclosure gives no material for the frame, no form for the hinge, no form for the radial guide, no facing for the jaw pad, no form for the carriage spring, no geometry for the complementary drive faces, and no form for the spring stack; it also never states that the hinge and latch must return the halves to a repeatable closed position. Common engineering plausibility is not source support for any of them.
findings.evidence: ¶7: "may be machined, cast, molded or fabricated from metal or from a reinforced polymer"; "The hinge 16 may be a pin hinge, a pair of interleaved knuckles on a common pin, or a flexible hinge section integral with the frame"; "the hinge 16 and the releasable latch 18 are arranged to bring the two frame halves to a repeatable closed position rather than merely to hold them near one another." ¶11: "may be a threaded pad, a dovetail, a flange with fastener holes". ¶15: "may be a rectangular slideway, a pair of parallel rails, or a bore that receives a cylindrical shank of the jaw carriage 22". ¶17: "may be faced with an elastomer, with a soft metal, or with a friction material". ¶19: "may be a compression spring seated in the radial guide 24, a tension spring acting between the jaw carriage 22 and the frame, or a leaf element". ¶31: "may be plain abutment faces lying in radial planes, faces inclined so that one segment end laps the other, or a tongue on one segment received in a recess of the other". ¶43: "may be a stack of disc springs, a nest of helical compression springs, or a single compression spring, selected to a chosen preload and rate."
findings.fix: Delete each quoted alternatives sentence and the "repeatable closed position" sentence, leaving the parts named and functionally related exactly as the disclosure states them. In ¶31 retain only the disclosed requirement that each pair of faces transmits circumferential drive in the closed frame and separates when the halves are swung apart.

findings.title: Mounting-boss load path into the jaw pads is an added assertion
findings.detail: The disclosure limits itself to "The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization." The candidate converts that into an affirmative load-path statement — reaction through the frame and into the jaw pads, and immunity of the jaw setting from an applied moment — which no source states.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶11: "A load applied to the mounting boss 66 is therefore reacted through the frame and into the jaw pads, and is not carried by the cam drive, so a moment applied by a carried instrument does not disturb the setting of the jaws." Summary ¶15: "so a load applied to the mounting boss is carried by the frame and does not disturb the cam drive." Disclosure: "The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization."
findings.fix: Replace the ¶11 sentence and the Summary ¶15 trailing clause with the disclosed statement: "The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22." (already present earlier in ¶11).

findings.title: Carriage springs rotating the cam ring back on release is an added mechanism, and claim 13 recites it
findings.detail: The disclosure's release sequence is that "releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened." It does not say the carriage springs drive the cam ring backwards through the slots, nor that the wedge retreats from the ring drive face. The candidate asserts a reverse drive train and claims it. I note this is arguably entailed by the disclosed follower-in-slot kinematics, which is why I have marked it major rather than critical, but as written it is an affirmative mechanism statement the sources do not make.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶53: "The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 54, and the carriage springs 42 rotate the cam ring 30 back through the oblique slots 38 and retract the jaw carriages 22". Claim 13: "wherein the carriage springs rotate the coupled cam ring back through the oblique slots and retract the jaw carriages outward when the releasable latch is released."

findings.title: FIG. 1 brief puts the jaw carriages in direct contact with the pipe, contradicting the description

The FIG. 1 brief instead ends each carriage block on the pipe circle so that block and pipe touch, with no pad drawn between them. That is visible geometry contradicting the text. (I could not check the rendered sheet: no rendered-*.png exists in figures/ and review/figure-audit-evidence.json is absent from this workspace.)

findings.detail: The inventor states a four-part essential relationship, one part of which is that the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel. Claim 1 recites coupling by closure, latch-driven ring rotation and slot synchronization but not the spring stack, which appears only in dependent claim 2. Independent method claim 19 does the same, with the stack appearing only in claim 20. Flagging as minor because each recited element of claim 1 is itself disclosed; the concern is that the claim as a whole covers a clamp the disclosure never presents, namely one whose latch travel is not force limited.

findings.title: Claim terms that never appear in the description for the same element
findings.detail: Four claim terms name elements or states the description names differently, so the same thing has two names across the document. findings.title: Claim 9 recites "the distribution of the jaw carriages" without antecedent basis

findings.title: Latch pivot and the line of action of the clamping load are added detail
findings.detail: The disclosure names only "a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe". The candidate explains the over-centre condition by introducing a pivot of the releasable latch — a part that appears nowhere else in the draft, in numerals.md, or in either source — and by asserting where the clamping load line of action falls relative to it. findings.fix: Delete that clause, leaving "The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20."

data.summary: The draft is internally coherent in its naming and its mechanics, and the four figure briefs agree with each other and with the numeral table (12 = upper half / first cam-ring segment 32 at upper left, 14 = lower half / second segment 34 at bottom; hinge end = left = faces 44/46; latch end = right = faces 48/50). No pixel-level figure review was possible: figures/ contains only the four Markdown briefs, there are no rendered-*.png files, and review/figure-audit-evidence.json does not exist in this workspace, so every figure finding below is against the brief text only. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references ("(none)") and the draft contains no [REF:...] citation, so there is no citation fidelity defect to report — but the Background's characterisations of bolt/toggle/band closures, individually wound jaws and nominal-diameter clamps rest on no source in the workspace, and the art supplied to this draft may be incomplete. The dominant problem is disclosure fidelity: the inventor's disclosure and the single-message conversation are one page long and identical to one another, yet the detailed description adds a substantial layer of structure, alternatives, load paths and performance results that neither source states — an over-center link (numeral 68, claimed in claim 5), a 2-into-1 split of the radial guides between frame halves (claim 8), a pad pivot axis orientation (claim 14), a roller follower (claim 15), indicator-pin mounting detail (claim 4), stroke-limiting structures (claim 12), a drive lug on the cam ring that also drives the FIG. 3 geometry, and several asserted results (self-centering, load reaction away from the split line, spring-stack preload relationship, positioning along the pipe in the first latch position, claim 22). Ten dependent claims and one method claim rest on those additions. Claim/description terminology drift ("closed condition", "assembly", "uncoupled", "resisted") and one antecedent-basis slip in claim 9 are minor by comparison.

findings.title: Over-center link 68 is a structural element no source discloses, and claim 5 recites it
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶43; draft/09-claims.md claim 5; draft/numerals.md numeral 68; figures/fig-04.md

findings.title: Two-guides-in-one-half / one-in-the-other distribution is unsupported, and claim 8 recites it

findings.title: Widening from the disclosed three carriages to "more than three", plus an added three-point rationale

findings.title: Indicator-pin mounting and housing opening are unsupported, and claim 4 recites them
